external_sources.title: Article 6ter: How International Law Protects EUCLID's Name and Emblem - EUCLID (Euclid University)
external_sources.content:
Countries bound by Article 6ter must refuse or invalidate the registration of trademarks that contain or imitate a protected name or emblem, unless the organization has authorized it. They must also prohibit its unauthorized use as a trademark where that use would suggest a connection with the organization that does not exist, or would mislead the public. In practical terms, no one may legitimately present a business, a diploma mill or a lookalike website under the EUCLID name or emblem. [...] The procedure is public and documented. The organization asks WIPO to communicate its signs to the States party to the Paris Convention and to the members of the WTO. WIPO publishes the communication in its Article 6ter Express database, and the date of publication counts as the date of receipt for every country. Each State then has twelve months in which it may object. Once communicated, the signs are protected in every State that has not objected.

## What the protection means in practice [...] Article 6ter is not a trademark and cannot be bought or registered by a company, a foundation or a private university. It exists to protect the symbols of public international authority. A State may communicate its own emblems; an intergovernmental organization, created by an agreement between States, may communicate its name, abbreviation and emblem. A purely private institution has no access to this mechanism, whatever its size or reputation.

The provision applies equally to armorial bearings, flags, other emblems, [...] Under Article 6 ter, each member country or international intergovernmental organization (IGO) may communicate armorial bearings, emblems, official signs and hallmarks indicating warranty and control, and names and abbreviations of IGOs to the IB, who will transmit the communications to the other member countries. Within twelve months from receipt of the notification, a member country may transmit its objections, through the IB. [...] other emblems, abbreviations, and names of international intergovernmental organizations of which one or more countries of the Union are members, except for those that are already the subject of international agreements in force, intended to ensure their protection (e.g., "Red Cross" and emblems protected by the Geneva Convention of August 12, 1949).
